title: Mary Wollstonecraft and her Vindication of the Rights of Woman
quote: She saw women get married and disappear.
deck: Beauty as survival. Dependence dressed as love. Mary saw the machinery—and wrote back.
credit: Mary Wollstonecraft, portrait c. 1797. Source: Wikipedia.
pages: Few days back I wrote about an AI ad selling women the oldest lie in a new little jar: that our bodies are unfinished until a man can look at them and approve.

A product for bigger breasts. A young woman made insecure, then made beautiful, then made lovable. Her boyfriend smiling because the problem has been fixed. And of course I was raging and thinking about Mary Wollstonecraft.

Because in 1792, two hundred and thirty-four years before our phones learned exactly which insecurity to serve us before breakfast, she was already writing about this. Not the tit patches. There were probably less of those to buy, though I wouldn’t be surprised if women didn’t use some home made plant applications for that purpose. But the whole societal machinery underneath this topic.

Women were raised to think beauty was their form of power, because nobody was planning to give them any real power. The way girls were trained to be charming instead of capable, delicate instead of educated, desirable instead of free. Women couldn’t conceivable be free, so they had to do anything they could to please a man enough to marry them. Back then, a woman could spend her whole life trying to become pleasing enough to survive the men around her and still be told that dependence was love. Actually, strike that, it’s still happening.
But Mary Wollstonecraft looked at all this two hundred years ago and said: this is not femininity. This is a trap. Then she wrote a book about it.
Men were less pleased, as you imagine, and called her a hyena in petticoats.
Obviously.

Mary was born in London in 1759, the second of seven children, into a family that had money once and then did what so many men do with money once it reaches their hands: her father managed to turn it into chaos.

Edward Wollstonecraft inherited enough to make the family comfortable. He tried farming, then failed at farming, moved them from place to place, lost more money, so he drank, raged, and made their home unsafe. Mary later remembered sleeping outside her mother’s bedroom to stop him from getting in and doing things he should not do.
Her brother Ned got a proper education, he was a man so it was expected.

He got inheritance money too. Mary, on the other side, was reserved the kind of education many girls got: a bit here, a bit there, enough reading to be respectable, not enough independence to become a liability.

But Mary was a liability, so she kept reading. She taught herself. She read the Bible, Shakespeare, Milton, philosophy. She learned languages. Later she translated from French, German, and Dutch. She became one of those women who makes people uncomfortable because she has not been successfully convinced to exist as decor.
Her choices, as a poor woman with no family safety net, were the standard options: companion, governess, teacher, wife if she could find the right man and call that an end to it.

She was not convinced of the latter, so she tried the first three. At nineteen, she worked as a paid companion to an older woman. She had to return home to nurse her dying mother. When her sister Eliza became trapped in a marriage that appeared to be destroying her, Mary helped her leave. The sisters went into hiding, makes you wonder why but you already know. Eliza
had to leave her baby behind and it unfortunately died without maternal protection. Bet you’ve stopped asking why by now, right?

Mary did not arrive at feminism because she had read a nice book about equality and thought it sounded fair. She watched what happened all around her, when women had no money, no education, no legal personhood, no route out of a bad home except running and hoping the people looking for them did not catch up.
She saw women get married and disappear.
She started a school with her sisters and her closest friend, Fanny Blood.
Fanny was clever, artistic, emotionally intense. Mary loved her fiercely. When Fanny married and moved to Portugal, Mary travelled there to help her during pregnancy.

Fanny died in childbirth, along with her baby. Mary came home ruined in all possible ways. The school failed too, so instead of finally getting married to some bloke who’d make “an honest woman” out of her, she did the thing women were not supposed to do unless they wanted to be called difficult, unfeminine, or insane. She became a professional writer.
She wrote children’s books, novels, educational manuals, political pamphlets.
She reviewed hundreds of books, translated some, and generally wrote to make money, granted one of the quickest ways for a woman’s intellect to become suspicious.
Then, when the French Revolution happened, Edmund Burke wrote a long, sentimental defense of hierarchy and aristocracy, and Mary Wollstonecraft wrote back.

Her Vindication of the Rights of Men came out in 1790. It was one of the first serious replies to Burke. At first it was anonymous. But the second edition came out with her name attached. She was thirty-one and entered the political conversation as a woman that refused to be decorative in it.
Two years later she wrote the book that made the world remember her, badly at first and then, much later, correctly. A Vindication of the Rights of Woman.

Title page of the 1792 American edition of Mary Wollstonecraft’s A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: With Strictures on Political and Moral Subjects. The facing page contains an inscription by women’s suffragist Susan B. Anthony.

Library of Congress Rare Book and Special Collections Division Washington, D.C. 20540 USA The title sounds almost polite now. It was savage then. People were outraged. Mary’s argument was not “please let women have a little more freedom when convenient”, but: you have built an entire civilization on raising half the population to be stupid on purpose, and then you use their manufactured weakness as proof that they should remain subordinate.

“TO M. TALLEYRAND-PERIGORD LATE BISHOP OF AUTUN Sir, Having read with great pleasure a pamphlet* which you have lately published. I dedicate this volume to you; to induce you to reconsider the subject, and maturely weigh what I have advanced respecting the rights of woman and national education: and I call with the firm tone of humanity;* for my arguments, Sir, are dictated by a disinterested spirit—I plead for my sex—not for myself. Independence I have long considered as the grand blessing of life, the basis of every virtue—and independence I will ever secure by contracting my wants, though I were to live on a barren heath.
It is then an affection for the whole human race that makes my pen dart rapidly along to support what I believe to be the cause of virtue: and the same motive leads me earnestly to wish to see woman

placed in a station in which she would advance, instead of retarding, the progress of those glorious principles that give a substance to morality. [..] Women are told from their infancy, and taught by the example of their mothers, that a little knowledge of human weakness, justly termed cunning, softness or temper, outward obedience, and a scrupulous attention to a puerile kind of propriety, will obtain for them the protection of man; and should they be beautiful, every thing else is needless, for, at least, twenty years of their lives.

Thus Milton describes our first frail mother; though when he tells us that women are formed for softness and sweet attractive grace, I cannot comprehend his meaning, unless, in the true Mahometan strain,* he meant to deprive us of souls, and insinuate that we were beings only designed by sweet attractive grace, and docile blind obedience, to gratify the senses of man when he can no longer soar on the wing of contemplation.* How grossly do they insult us who thus advise us only to render ourselves gentle, domestic brutes!”
Mary raged against a society that asked women to obsess over beauty, obedience, flirtation, and marriage. That kept them financially dependent.

That denied them serious education. That made them compete for male approval because male approval is the currency they need to survive, then looked at the resulting anxiety, vanity, weakness, insecurity, and called it female nature.
Mary called bullshit.
She argued that women should be educated alongside men. That they should learn practical skills and be able to support themselves and their children.
That they could be doctors too, not only nurses. That they should participate in politics. That women should never have to marry just because they can’t afford not to.

She didn’t want women to become men, bus simply allowed that women to become human. And that was the whole problem, because a human woman can leave, she can say no, she can ask questions and demand answers.
Mary herself was not some clean little statue of reason standing above the mess of life in a white dress. No sir, she fell in love. Badly. And more than once.

In 1792, she became infatuated with the painter Henry Fuseli, a married man known for painting nightmares and demons, which should perhaps have been a clue. Mary proposed that she, Fuseli, and his wife Sophia live together in a ménage à trois. Sophia, obviously, said no, most likely while clutching her pearls.
The exciting thing is that Mary was trying to imagine a life outside the tiny approved box. She spent years writing about marriage as the economic
prison for women. She did not suddenly become a hypocrite because she wanted intimacy without surrendering herself to it.
Fuseli’s wife rejected the arrangement, so Mary left England and went to Paris alone, in the middle of the Revolution, having already decided ordinary levels of drama were for other people.

There she met Gilbert Imlay, an American merchant and adventurer. They became lovers. To protect her during the Terror, when British citizens were at risk, she was registered as his wife. They never really married, but she had a daughter, Fanny. Some names, you want with you all your life.

Then Imlay did what disappointing men have been doing since the invention of doors: he started drifting. He was unfaithful, made promises and did not keep them. Mary, who had written so fiercely about the need for women not to depend on men, found herself devastated by one.

She attempted suicide twice in 1795. A part that people love to use against women like Mary. See? Too emotional. Too much. Not rational enough. All that writing about independence, and look what happened when she loved somebody. Yes, love dumbs us all, but that is not the lesson.

Emotional independence is not a switch that women can flick after centuries of being trained to survive through attachment. The lesson is that even the woman who wrote the clearest case for female self-sufficiency could still be broken by abandonment in a world designed to punish unmarried mothers, isolate women, and make love feel like the only available shelter under the sun. Mary did not fail her philosophy, she just proved why she needed it.

After Imlay, she travelled through Sweden, Norway, and Denmark with baby Fanny and a French maid, partly because Imlay sent her to handle one of his business disasters, also because even while abandoning her he had work for her to do.

She returned with a travel book that became one of the most beautiful things she wrote. Here’s an excerpt of her travels through Sweden: “The farms are small. Indeed most of the houses we saw on the road indicated poverty, or rather that the people could just live.
Towards the frontiers they grew worse and worse in their appearance, as if not willing to put sterility itself out of countenance.

No gardens smiled round the habitations, not a potato or cabbage to eat with the fish drying on a stick near the door. A little grain here and there appeared, the long stalks of which you might almost reckon. The day was gloomy when we passed over this rejected spot, the wind bleak, and winter seemed to be contending with nature, faintly struggling to change the season. Surely, thought I, if the sun ever shines here it cannot warm these stones; moss only cleaves to them, partaking of their hardness, and nothing like vegetable life appears to cheer with hope the heart.
So far from thinking that the primitive inhabitants of the world lived in a southern climate where Paradise spontaneously arose, I am led to

infer, from various circumstances, that the first dwelling of man happened to be a spot like this which led him to adore a sun so seldom seen; for this worship, which probably preceded that of demons or demigods, certainly never began in a southern climate, where the continual presence of the sun prevented its being considered as a good; or rather the want of it never being felt, this glorious luminary would carelessly have diffused its blessings without being hailed as a benefactor. Man must therefore have been placed in the north, to tempt him to run after the sun, in order that the different parts of the earth might be peopled. Nor do I wonder that hordes of barbarians always poured out of these regions to seek for milder climes, when nothing like cultivation attached them to the soil[..]” You can read this book for free online Then she met William Godwin again.
Godwin was a philosopher too. He had initially not liked her much. Which is a really good beginning for a relationship between two people who both have ideas and intend to use them.
They became lovers. They lived in separate adjoining houses for a while, keeping their independence, sending notes to each other [Ideal, I KNOW!!!].
They only married when Mary became pregnant again, partly to protect the legal status of their child.
On 30 August 1797, Mary gave birth to a daughter. Her name was Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin. She would grow up to write Frankenstein.

Ten days later, Mary Wollstonecraft the mother died from complications of childbirth. She was thirty-eight. She wrote all her adult life about women’s education, women’s work, women’s dependence, women’s rights, the French Revolution, slavery, marriage, motherhood, reason, passion, imagination, violence, poverty, and the stupid waste of building a society where women had to become ornamental to be safe, then died doing the one thing society insisted was her proper destiny.
And the daughter she left behind became one of the most important writers in the world.

After Mary died, William Godwin wrote a memoir about her. He was trying to honor her. He also told the truth in a way that eighteenth-century society was never going to forgive. The affair, the unmarried child, the suicide attempts, her complicated love life. The fact that she had wanted more than one life can give a woman.
For much of the nineteenth century, people used Mary’s private life to dismiss Mary’s ideas. They did not have to argue seriously against her. They could just make her into a warning.

This is what women get when they speak too clearly. If you are obedient, you disappear, if you are brilliant, you are difficult, if you are sexual, you are discredited, if you are hurt, you are unstable and ought to calm yourself down. And if you are angry, you are a hyena in petticoats, as the English writer Horace Walpole named her after she published her Vindication.

Mary Wollstonecraft knew that women were being trained to find their value in being wanted. She knew that the prettiest cage is still a cage. And she knew that a woman can’t be a full person if every part of her survival depends on pleasing somebody else.
More than two hundred years passed and the pitch is still the same for women living in a patriarchal society. Mary called it all the way back then, and we are still trying to catch up.
sources: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792); A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790); Letters Written during a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark (1796); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Mary Wollstonecraft”; Benjamin Colbert, “Mary Wollstonecraft,” British Travel Writing; Barbara Taylor, Mary Wollstonecraft: Philosophy, Passion, and Politics (2020); Janet Todd, Mary Wollstonecraft: A Revolutionary Life (2000).

title: Olympe de Gouges and the illusion of universal rights
quote: “Man, are you capable of being fair? A woman is asking: at least you will allow her that right. Tell me? What gave you the sovereign right to oppress my sex?”
deck: A republic proclaimed universal rights. Olympe asked it to mean what it said.
credit: Portrait of Olympe de Gouges. Source: Wikimedia.
pages: Once upon a time, there was a small butcher’s house in Montauban, in the south of France. The year was 1748. A girl was born to the butcher and a servant woman. They named her Marie Gouze.

She grew up speaking Occitan, the language of the region, considered provincial and inferior by Parisian elites. She received almost no formal education. She was poor and female, which in 18th-century France meant the state barely registered her existence.

She was married off at sixteen to a man much older than herself. Her husband died and she refused to carry his name into the future. She took her mother's middle name, invented an aristocratic particle no one gave her, renamed herself Olympe de Gouges, and moved to Paris to become a playwright. Now you may not be impressed with this, but remember that a woman in eighteenth-century France existed legally as a derivative noun: first *fille de*, then *femme de*, then *veuve de*. Daughter of, wife of, widow of.
She was always someone's grammatical appendage. Olympe de Gouges decided she was to be a subject. She didn't even ask permission.

Portrait of Olympe de Gouges - Wikimedia She didn’t write well, technically. Her French was Occitan-infected, grammatically non-standard. She dictated most of her texts because writing by hand was difficult. The Comédie Française, the most prestigious theatre in France, was controlled by a small group of men who had run it as a private fiefdom since the 1680s. In the 200 years they’d been in operation, they had accepted 2,627 plays into their repertory. Seventy-seven were by women.
That’s just under 3%.
She got hers in. It was one of the rarest achievements for a woman in that era.

Olympe didn’t just fight to have her plays staged. She fought publicly, loudly, in pamphlets she printed at her own expense and pasted on the walls of Paris. She wrote about slavery, about women’s rights, about divorce, about the children of unwed mothers, about debt imprisonment. At a time when most women who wrote did so anonymously (Madame de Staël published her political texts on the Revolution without her name, Madame Roland circulated her thoughts in private letters), Olympe de Gouges put her name on everything.
On August 26, 1789, the National Assembly adopted the Déclaration des droits de l’homme et du citoyen, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The word used was hommes. Men.

Two years later, as it became painfully clear that the “universal” citizen of the Revolution was in fact going to be a French, propertied male over twenty-five, Olympe de Gouges sat down and rewrote the entire document, article by article.

She published it on September 14, 1791, the exact same day as the ratification of the new constitution. She titled it Déclaration des droits de la femme et de la citoyenne and, with boldness, dedicated it to Queen Marie
Antoinette, a deeply ironic gesture, given the Queen’s unpopularity at the time. Olympe hoped the Queen might use her influence to support the rights of women.

First page of Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen - Wikipedia The document opens with a sharp question: “Man, are you capable of being fair? A woman is asking: at least you will allow her that right. Tell me? What gave you the sovereign right to oppress my sex?”
She doesn’t explain why he’s wrong. She asks whether he’s capable of being fair. She lets him sit with that for a second. Then comes the demonstration.

Article X is the one that became famous, partly because of what happened to her two years later: “La femme a le droit de monter sur l’échafaud; elle doit avoir également celui de monter à la Tribune.”
The woman that has the right to mount the scaffold, must equally have the right to mount the podium.

She was pointing at the logical obscenity of a system that holds women legally responsible enough to execute, but not responsible enough to vote. If you can drag us to the guillotine for crimes against the state, then we are subjects of the state. And subjects of the state have political rights. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot kill us for breaking your laws while telling us we don’t have the agency to make them.

Olympe’s article XI gave women the right to publicly name the fathers of their children. “Any Citizen can thus say freely: I am the mother of your child, without being forced by barbarous prejudice to hide the truth.” In 1791 she was demanding paternity accountability. France won’t have anything like it for another two centuries.
Article XVI: any constitution drafted without the participation of the majority of its citizens is null and void. No constitution without women is a real constitution.

In the postamble, she proposed replacing marriage with a civil contract between equals, property held in common, children acknowledged regardless of which “bed they come from,” dissolution available to either party. She was describing something close to modern civil union law. In 1791.
Then she closed with a war cry:
“Woman, wake up; the alarm bell of reason rings across the universe; recognize your rights.”

She also insisted, against Robespierre and the Jacobins who were busy building their vision of universal republican virtue out of very masculine bodies, that the Revolution was not authored by nature or by God. It was authored by human beings. Fallible, self-interested, embodied human beings.
And as long as only some of those humans were allowed to co-author it, it was not what it claimed to be, and that is, Universal.

The men of the National Assembly mostly ignored her Declaration. Some laughed. To them, the idea of applying universal rights to women was not a radical extension of their own logic, it was a joke. The notion that the subject of the Declaration was not gender-neutral, that “l’homme” had always meant men specifically, was not something they were considering.

She was arrested on July 20, 1793, the same day I was born, almost two centuries later. The official charge was sedition: she had posted pamphlets around Paris calling for a referendum on whether France should be a monarchy, a federation, or a republic. But she had also been offering to defend Louis XVI at his trial, and publicly attacking Robespierre, and writing a play that dared to represent Marie-Antoinette as a complex human being rather than a pornographic monster.
At her trial, she was legally entitled to a defense lawyer. The judge denied her this right, claiming: “You have enough wits to defend yourself on your own.”

She performed her innocence brilliantly. A spectator at the trial recorded that as the charges were read, she joined her hands repeatedly and rolled her eyes toward the ceiling, then showed surprise, then looked straight at the audience and smiled. The audience, according to another spectator, would have acquitted her if the judges hadn’t cut her off.
The judges did not acquit her.

When she was in prison and the regime of Terror was fully underway, she wrote from her cell: “Republican laws promised us that no illegal authority would strike citizens; yet an arbitrary act has stripped me of my liberty in the middle of a free people... Is freedom of opinion and the press not consecrated as the most precious heritage of man? Do these rights present only illusory meaning?”
She already knew the answer.
She was executed on the afternoon of November 3, 1793. On the scaffold, she addressed the crowd gathered to watch: “Children of the Fatherland, you will avenge my death.”

A few days later, the radical Jacobin politician Pierre-Gaspard Chaumette gave a speech warning republican women who dared to question their assigned roles. He used Olympe de Gouges as his warning: “Remember that virago, that woman-man, the impudent Olympe de Gouges, who abandoned all the cares of her household because she wanted to engage in politics and commit crimes. This forgetfulness of the virtues of her sex led her to the scaffold.”
Forgetfulness of the virtues of her sex.

She had forgotten to be silent. She had forgotten to stay home. She had forgotten that public speech was a masculine prerogative and that a woman who claimed it was not a woman making a political argument but a woman making a category error.

Shortly after her execution, women’s clubs were dissolved. It became illegal for women to gather in groups of more than five. The Society of Revolutionary Republican Women, the organization that had been the most active female political club of the Revolution, was abolished. The women who had literally marched on Versailles, who had been in the Revolution, were erased from it.

The Déclaration des droits de la femme et de la citoyenne was written in 1791. For nearly two centuries it remained largely forgotten, a footnote, if mentioned at all, while French schoolchildren were taught about the “universal” rights of man. It was not until the 1970s and especially the 1980s, with the rise of modern feminism and the work of historians like Olivier Blanc, that the text was properly republished and Olympe de Gouges began to be recognized as the radical thinker she was.

Marie Gouze, daughter of a butcher, a widow at seventeen, died as Olympe de Gouges, playwright, pamphleteer, feminist, guillotined by a republic that claimed to have invented the universal rights she spent her life demanding it honor. She was also a mother. She raised her only son, Pierre, alone and helped launch him into a military career. The Revolution would later put their bond under terrible strain.
She mounted the scaffold. She was right all along: she had the right to mount the podium too.

Her body was thrown into a mass grave at the Madeleine Cemetery. Like so many others executed during the Terror, her remains were later lost, possibly transferred to the Paris Catacombs among thousands of unidentified bones.
There is no grave marker or stone for visitors to read.
Women like Olympe are what Dead Women Society digs for.
sources: Janie Vanpée, “Performing Justice: The Trials of Olympe de Gouges” (Theatre Journal, 1999); Joan Wallach Scott, “French Feminists and the Rights of ‘Man’: Olympe de Gouges’s Declarations” (History Workshop, 1989); Joshua Rivas, “The Radical Novelty of Olympe de Gouges” (Nottingham French Studies, 2014); Olympe de Gouges, Écrits politiques, ed. Olivier Blanc (Côté-femmes, 1993).

title: The Sun Queen: Mária Telkes and the Sun she tried to tame
quote: Most people would have moved on. Mária doubled down.
deck: She wanted sunlight to change everyday life. First, she had to fight for room to work.
credit: Mária Telkes with experimental equipment. Source: NREL, U.S. Department of Energy.
pages: “The important thing is not to stop questioning. Curiosity has its own reason for existence. One cannot help but be in awe when he contemplates the mysteries of eternity, of life, of the marvelous structure of reality. It is enough if one tries merely to comprehend a little of this mystery each day.” - Albert Einstein For the entirety of my life, even during the long winters in Northern Sweden, at one point in the day the Sun comes up. Every day, every single day of my stay on this Earth, I have been graced with the light of our star, the Sun.

It produces, every second, more energy than humanity has consumed in the entirety of its existence on this planet. It does it reliably, without sending anyone an invoice, and has been doing so for approximately four and a half billion years. It will continue doing so for roughly another five billion, at which point it will expand into a red giant and incinerate the Earth. But that is not really my problem, or yours.

The remarkable thing is not that we eventually figured out how to use it (solar power, that is). The remarkable thing is how long it took us, and how hard certain people worked to make sure the woman who got closest to solving it first didn’t get the credit she deserved.
That woman was Mária Telkes.

Born in Budapest in 1900, Mária grew up in a family unusual for the era: they let her be curious. As a girl of ten or eleven, she conducted chemistry experiments in a garden shed and once produced a small explosion. Most families would have taken this as a sign to redirect their daughter toward more suitable pursuits. Her father took it as a sign she was onto something interesting.

She studied physical chemistry at the University of Budapest and earned her doctorate in 1924, an extraordinary achievement at a time when women in European science departments were so rare they were sometimes treated as clerical errors. A book on alternative energy sources that Mária read as a freshman at the University of Budapest sparked her lifelong fascination with solar energy and laid the foundation for her pioneering career.

“The book explained that the usual energy sources have geographical limitations, especially in the less-developed tropical regions, but the sun is directly overhead in the tropics, and you do not have to explore for it”, she said later.
Mária envisioned a future in which people in developing countries could meet their basic needs through freely available solar energy, and she was determined to help bring that vision to life.

After earning a doctorate in physical chemistry in 1924, she remained at the University of Budapest as an instructor before immigrating to the United States, then at the forefront of solar energy research. In 1928, she joined the Cleveland Clinic Foundation, a young nonprofit academic medical center, as a biophysicist.

For nearly a decade, Mária worked with surgeon and scientist George Washington Crile on experimental biophysics research. Although the work had little to do with solar energy, it established her reputation as a gifted researcher and inventor.
It was during her time at the clinic that she first attracted media attention.

Although reporters initially showed interest in the foundation’s scientific advances, coverage often drifted away from the research itself and toward more superficial subjects, a pattern that would follow her throughout much of her career.

In 1932, syndicated columnist Arthur Brisbane, whom newspaper editors of the era described as “the most highly paid and most widely read editorial writer in the world,” visited the clinic to write about its work. Yet rather than focusing on the groundbreaking research being conducted there, Brisbane devoted much of his column to remarks about Mária’s appearance, personality, and his unsuccessful attempts to charm her. Some things never change.

While working at the Cleveland Clinic, Mária continued pursuing solar energy research in her spare time, developing a thermopile capable of converting sunlight into electricity. The invention attracted national attention and established her as a rising figure in the field.
Solar-energy pioneer Mária Telkes with experimental energy-conversion equipment. Source: National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), U.S.
Department of Energy.

After becoming an American citizen in 1937, she joined Westinghouse as a research engineer studying the conversion of heat into electricity. When she learned about MIT’s new Solar Energy Conversion Project, she immediately sought a position. Her initial application was unsuccessful, but Mária refused to be overlooked. She traveled to Massachusetts and personally demonstrated her thermopile to the project’s all-male selection committee, arguing that it was far more efficient than existing solar technologies. Her persistence paid off: in 1939, MIT invited her to join the program, giving her a place among the nation’s leading solar energy researchers.

Ironically, the MIT program was led by chemical engineering professor Hoyt Hottel, who remained deeply skeptical that solar energy could ever become a practical source of power. While she saw the sun as an untapped solution to humanity’s energy needs, Hottel viewed such optimism with suspicion, a divide that would persist throughout their careers.

Any debate over solar energy’s future was soon overshadowed by global events. After the United States entered World War II, MIT’s research priorities shifted toward the war effort. Mária joined the Office of Scientific Research and Development as a civilian advisor and was tasked with solving a life-or- death problem. Allied pilots and sailors stranded at sea often survived crashes or sinkings, only to die of dehydration before rescue could arrive.
Surrounded by seawater they could not drink, they needed a portable source of fresh water.
Mária believed solar energy could provide one. Inspired by a jellyfish she spotted while sailing, she designed a portable solar still, a lightweight,
inflatable device that used sunlight to convert seawater into fresh drinking water. It required no fuel, electricity, or moving parts, making it ideal for emergency survival kits.
U.S. service members demonstrate Mária Telkes’ solar still. Source: Mária Telkes Papers, Design and the Arts Special Collections, Arizona State University Library.

The U.S. government was impressed enough to order 100,000 units. Yet, once again, Mária faced resistance. Production became bogged down by delays at MIT, where project director Hoyt Hottel repeatedly revised specifications and changed manufacturers. By the end of the war, none of the ordered stills had been delivered. Although the invention arrived too late to aid the wartime effort, it was eventually incorporated into military emergency kits and remained in use for years afterward. An unknowable number of pilots and sailors likely survived because of Mária’s innovation.
Mária Telkes’ solar still, a lightweight device folded into a compact package that required no fuel or electricity. Source: Mária Telkes Papers, Arizona State
University Library.

After the war, Mária turned her attention to what many considered solar energy’s greatest unsolved challenge: storage. Capturing sunlight was one thing. Storing its heat for use at night or during cloudy weather was another.

She proposed an experimental solar house that would use Glauber’s salt, a heat-storing compound, to absorb solar energy during the day and release it after sunset. Despite skepticism from her supervisor, Hoyt Hottel, MIT approved the project and built the house in 1946.

The experiment failed. The salt corroded its containers, causing leaks that rendered the system unusable. Mária blamed poor operation of the test house. Her colleagues blamed the design. The disagreement escalated, and Hottel removed her from the solar project.
Most people would have moved on.
Mária doubled down.

In 1948, working with architect Eleanor Raymond and philanthropist Amelia Peabody, she helped build the Dover Sun House in Massachusetts, the first house heated primarily through stored solar energy. Using an improved version of her thermal-storage concept, the house demonstrated that solar heating could work on a practical scale.
“Sunlight will be used as a source of energy sooner or later anyway. Why wait?,” she wrote in 1951.

Mária Telkes at the Dover Sun House in Massachusetts, completed in 1948. Developed with architect Eleanor Raymond and funded by philanthropist Amelia Peabody, the experimental home used solar energy and thermal storage to provide heat, making it one of the world’s most famous early solar-powered houses. Source: Mária Telkes Papers, Design and the Arts Special Collections, Arizona State University Library.
Newspapers celebrated it. Visitors traveled from across the country to see it.
For a brief moment, it seemed possible that the United States might embrace solar energy decades before the energy crises of the 1970s.
The Dover Sun House - Source: Mária Telkes Papers, Design and the Arts Special Collections, Arizona State University Library.
It didn’t.

Many researchers, including Hottel, remained unconvinced that solar energy could compete economically with cheap oil and gas. Mária disagreed. She saw solar power not simply as a technical challenge, but as a way to reduce dependence on finite fuels and expand access to energy. Once again, her vision put her at odds with the scientific establishment. Although the Dover Sun House became an international sensation, Mária found herself increasingly marginalized at MIT and eventually pushed out of the project she had helped pioneer.
The story, however, was not as triumphant as the newspaper headlines suggested.
Within a few years, the Dover Sun House began to struggle. Components failed. The heating system proved expensive to operate. Eventually, a conventional oil furnace had to be installed.

Back at MIT, relations between Mária and Hoyt Hottel had deteriorated beyond repair. Colleagues complained that she was stubborn and unwilling to submit to authority. Mária argued that her work was being judged unfairly and that many of the project’s problems stemmed from poor implementation rather than flawed ideas. In 1953, after years of conflict, MIT fired her.
For a moment, it appeared that both Mária and her vision of solar-powered homes had been defeated.
Neither stayed down for long.

Over the following decades, Mária continued inventing. She directed solar- energy laboratories, accumulated more than twenty patents, and remained one of the world's most outspoken advocates for solar power.
Then, in the 1970s, she got another chance.

At the University of Delaware’s Institute of Energy Conversion, Mária helped develop Solar One, an experimental house that successfully generated both heat and electricity from the sun. Unlike the Dover Sun House, Solar One benefited from advances in materials, engineering, and photovoltaic technology that had not existed a generation earlier. The future Mária had spent decades arguing for was finally beginning to arrive.

She was described as emotional. Difficult. Uncooperative. These are familiar words used against women who refuse to subordinate their judgment to men who, on the evidence, are less accomplished than they are. She was also described as: Mária continued inventing, publishing, and advocating through her seventies and eighties. She received recognition from engineering societies and the Smithsonian, and was eventually celebrated as a pioneer of solar energy, a visionary, a woman ahead of her time.

“Her mind was somewhere else, it was not on these everyday things. She did not cook, she did not sew. She was a visionary and thinking about projects and problems,and the other things didn’t matter.” - Joy Olgyay
Perhaps Mária’s most enduring legacy was not the solar house or the solar still, but a far simpler invention: the solar oven.

Decades before terms like “energy poverty” entered the mainstream, Mária understood that billions of people lived beneath abundant sunlight while lacking reliable access to fuel. In many communities, cooking required hours spent gathering wood, accelerating deforestation and exposing families to dangerous smoke from indoor fires.

Mária Telkes demonstrates her solar oven, a low-cost cooker powered entirely by sunlight. Designed for regions with limited access to conventional fuels, the oven reflected her belief that solar energy could improve everyday life for people around the world. Source: Mária Telkes Papers, Design and the Arts Special Collections, Arizona State University Library.

After her death, scientists working in Central America and Africa found that Mária’s insight had been remarkably prescient. Programs teaching families to build and use solar ovens often relied on versions of her designs because they were inexpensive, durable, and easy to adapt to local needs.

The benefits extended far beyond cooking. Families spent less money on fuel. Women and children spent less time gathering firewood. Homes had cleaner air. Communities used the time saved to pursue education, start businesses, and organize local projects.

This was the future Mária had imagined decades earlier: not solar energy as a technological curiosity, but as a practical tool that could improve everyday life for people with the fewest resources and the greatest need.

She died in Hungary in 1995, ten days before her ninety-fifth birthday, during her first visit to her homeland in more than seventy years. Despite decades of pioneering work and international recognition, Mária's death in Hungary in 1995 received so little attention in the United States that newspapers did not report it until the following year.

The phrase “ahead of her time” is one worth examining. It usually means a person was right while everyone around her was wrong, and that the wrongness lasted long enough to become a civilizational embarrassment.

Mária Telkes demonstrated practical solar thermal technology in an American house in 1948. She built solar-powered desalination systems during World War II. She designed solar ovens that are still improving lives decades after her death. Many of the ideas she spent her career defending are now standard components of the global transition to renewable energy.
Yet throughout that career she was forced to prove herself repeatedly.

Newspapers wrote about her appearance instead of her work. Male colleagues questioned her judgment, delayed her projects, removed her from leadership roles, and eventually pushed her out of institutions she had helped make relevant. Traits celebrated as brilliance and determination in male scientists were often described as stubbornness and insubordination in her.
It is impossible to know what Mária Telkes might have accomplished had she received the same support, funding, trust, and institutional backing routinely afforded to many of her male contemporaries.
What is easier to see is what she accomplished without them.

The sun, for its part, continued showing up every single morning, exactly as it always had: indifferent to egos, academic politics, and humanity’s remarkable talent for ignoring good ideas when they arrive in the wrong package.

title: Digging out Sisterage: Boston marriages and the medieval Beguines
quote: The Beguines found a third door.
deck: Shared homes, shared resources, lives outside male management. The precedents we were never taught.
pages: I wrote a while back about Sisterage, my view of how women can start to live together under the same roof, not as in a lesbian relationship (though honestly, if we could just choose orientation on a dropdown, patriarchy would have a much rougher time), but in a supporting, trusting, emotionally and financially balanced mutual agreement.

That idea didn’t come out of nowhere. It came from watching what really works when women choose each other without the constant negotiation, score-keeping, and invisible labor that so often defines mixed-gender households. And it feels more urgent now than ever, because the world outside those walls keeps reminding women why going it alone, or rather, building your life with women, makes sense.

Right now, women are still discriminated against in the workplace in ways that are both blatant and exhausting. We are paid less, often around 80% of men’s wages in full-time roles, with the gap barely shrinking in recent decades. Over a lifetime, that adds up to hundreds of thousands dollars in lost earnings. We have to work noticeably harder, perform better, and navigate more subjective bias just to be assessed as nearly as competent as our male colleagues. House making and caregiving responsibilities, which still fall disproportionately on women, further stall careers, contribute to stress and autoimmune disease and compound the penalty.

In the age of the “Rape Academy”, those public websites and group chats where men openly trade videos of rapes, tactics for drugging, assaulting, and And then there’s the deeper, more painful crisis of trust.

controlling women (including their own partners) while sharing tips on how to avoid consequences, and the endless parade of “Nice Guys” who perform sensitivity and progressiveness until they feel safe enough to reveal something much darker, many women are reaching a point of profound exhaustion.

While everyone was busy joking about whether a man or a bear is more dangerous, women were collecting real life trauma: surveys where up to half of women report at least one occasion of harassment or assault in outdoor spaces, stories of being followed or grabbed on trails, and now a term like “alpine divorce” for women abandoned or killed on hikes often enough for this new practice to need a name. In the same years you can count U.S. women attacked by bears in the tens, you count women raped, beaten, or killed by men in the millions. Of course we pick the bear.

And it’s not all men, of course. But enough. And the problem is that the dangerous ones are often the best at hiding it. They disguise their real personality remarkably well. They learn the language, say the right things, weaponize therapy-speak, and present as safe, evolved partners. So women are left carrying the mental load of constant vigilance: Not all men… but what if this one is? W hich simply qualifies all men as untrustworthy. What if the man I’m building a life with is one of the ones who would leave if I got seriously ill? (Studies have shown women with serious illnesses face a dramatically higher risk of partner abandonment than men in the same situation.)

What if the person I rely on for emotional and financial stability is keeping score in ways I won’t see until it’s too late? What if the man I live with drugs me and rapes me at night, streaming the entire thing for millions of other sick men to see, getting instructions from the chat on what to do next with my body?
What if my boss is watching me? What if my neighbor is watching me?
Who isn’t watching me get raped?

It’s not about hating men. It’s about refusing to keep subsidizing unequal labor, unequal risk, and unequal reliability with our time, money, health, and peace of mind. But this isn’t new. Women have built these households before, deliberately, in numbers large enough to threaten the men who counted on their dependence. And every time, the system found a way to make the arrangement disappear, not by banning it outright, but by renaming it, mocking it, pricing it out of reach, or simply waiting until everyone forgot the word.

In New England, between roughly 1870 and 1920, educated women started pairing off. They called it nothing, or they called it friendship, and later they called it a “Boston marriage”: two women sharing a home, finances, social life, sometimes a bed, for decades. Some were romantic. Some weren’t. The point was the structure: mutual support, shared labor, no male head of household, equality.
Women.
The most recent version was called Boston Marriages.

Sarah Orne Jewett - W ikipedia image Annie Adams Fields (1834 ‒ 1915), 1890, painting by John Singer Sargent / Credit: Boston Athenaeum Sarah Orne Jewett lived with Annie Fields for years, around six months of each year living and travelling together, after Annie’s husband died.
Mary Woolley, president of Mount Holyoke College, lived with Jeannette Marks for almost fifty years. These relationships were not secrets or

scandalous. They were visible, and that was possible because they were also respectable companionships. These women had money, education, social standing. The system tolerated them because they posed no threat to the larger architecture. A few rich white ladies living together in Cambridge? Fine.

But this is left out of the W ikipedia summary: Boston marriages were not a lesbian phenomenon, and they were not just an upper-class quirk. They were a structural response to a structural problem. In the late 19th century, women’s colleges were producing thousands of educated women with no intention of marrying. Because marriage, as legally constructed, meant coverture: a woman’s property became her husband’s, her legal existence suspended. If you had a degree, a career, a bank account, marriage was not a partnership. It was dissolution of the self.

So they didn’t. They paired off. They bought houses together. They combined incomes. They raised nieces and nephews, adopted children, built networks of care that functioned exactly like the families they were told they were failing to form. The term “Boston marriage” itself is a minimization, it makes the arrangement sound regional, quaint, temporary. It wasn’t. It was nationwide, it was decades-long, and it was deliberate.

The problem? It was only available to women who already had money and education. This is how patriarchy adapts: it doesn’t ban the exit. It prices it out of reach. W orking-class women still had to marry, still had to route their labor through men, still had to play the game. The sisterage became a privilege, not a right.

And then it was laughed out of existence. By the 1920s, the term “Boston marriage” was a punchline. By the 1950s, it was forgotten. By the time second- wave feminism arrived, women were reinventing the wheel, “consciousness- raising groups,” “communal households”, without knowing they were rebuilding what had already existed, what had already worked, what had already been mocked into silence.

For roughly four hundred years between the Boston marriages and anything earlier, the sisterage as a visible, collective structure disappeared from the record. It’s not that women never lived together, they always did, out of necessity, out of poverty, out of widowhood, but they were not allowed to name it. The shared houses were deemed “spinster households,” a term that made the arrangement sound like failure rather than choice. The women inside them became invisible by definition.
But let’s go back further. Way back in the medieval age, there was another word for it. And they built it at scale: the Beguines.

In the 12th century, across the Low Countries and into France and Germany, women started doing something the Church couldn’t categorize. They moved into shared houses called beguinages, in groups of ten, twenty, sometimes hundreds. They worked. They prayed, but not under any approved rule. They were single, widowed, sometimes married women who simply left. They took in laundry, brewed beer, copied manuscripts, cared for the sick, buried the dead. Many communities managed property, rents, and shared resources through locally recognized arrangements. They managed their own finances.
They existed outside the ordinary structures of husband-led households and formal convent obedience, though they still operated within medieval civic and ecclesiastical worlds.
The Church called them beguinae, a word that might come from beg (to pray).

The etymology is as erased as the women. What matters is what they were: a deliberate, permanent household formed by two or more women as platonic life partners, sharing domestic, financial, and emotional labor.
Sound familiar?
The medieval experim ent

They were not nuns. They took no vows. They could leave. They could marry, though many didn’t. They could own property, which under medieval law usually required either a husband or a convent. The Beguines found a third door. They walked through it in such numbers that by the 14th century, some beguinages housed thousands of women. In Bruges, in Ghent, in Amsterdam, entire districts centered on women’s communal life, with unusual degrees of female self-governance for the era.
And the men in power could not stand it.

The witch ‑ burning ages were often also maneuvers from the Church and patriarchy to ensure the land and money never went to people who would not serve, well, the Church and patriarchy. So it happened that every time a witch was burned, their land and fortune was passed to the Church or local noble.

So many women who tried and even made it on their own, by their own power, or by being widowed, were “discovered” to be witches and murdered for their possessions. Most of those witches were women who refused to obey and cede their possessions to a man, but some were men who simply had made a good life for themselves and refused to serve the Church and upper layer in hierarchy. The preferred target for witch title wasn’t just the wise woman with herbs. It wasn’t just the midwife who knew too much. It was the independent woman. The woman with property. The woman with a trade.
The woman who proved that male authority was optional.

The Burnings Women’s autonomy was rarely destroyed in one dramatic stroke. More often, it was eroded through a mix of law, theology, ridicule, surveillance, and fear. A household of women supporting one another could be tolerated in one century, then treated as suspicious in the next. What changed was not women’s desire for independence, but the patience patriarchal institutions had for it.
The Beguines learned this early.

As their communities grew in wealth, visibility, and influence, so did unease around them. These were women living outside the two approved scripts available to most medieval women: marriage or enclosure. They earned money, managed property, cared for the sick, educated girls, and formed durable networks of female mutual dependence that did not route authority through a husband or church representative. That alone made them difficult to classify.
In 1310, the patience ran out in Paris. They brought Marguerite Porete to the Place de Grève.

Marguerite was a Beguine, highly educated for that time, fiercely independent, and the author of a book called The Mirror of Simple Souls. In it, she argued something unforgivable: that a soul filled with divine love achieves a state of union with God so complete that it no longer needs the Church as a mediator. It doesn’t need priests. She bypassed the entire medieval hierarchy of male authority and claimed direct, unmediated access to the divine.
The Inquisitor of France called her a pseudo-mulier, a “fake woman.” Because a real woman, in their eyes, required management. A real woman submitted.

They arrested her. They held her in prison for a year and a half. During her entire trial, Marguerite refused to speak to the inquisitors. She refused to take their oaths. She refused to recant her book, even after they burned it in front of her. She simply looked at the men who demanded her submission, and she offered them silence.

On June 1, 1310, they burned her alive. The chronicles note that the crowd wept at how calmly she faced the fire. But patriarchy is thorough: after they burned her body, they kept her book. The Mirror of Simple Souls was translated and circulated widely for centuries, anonymously. It was attributed to male mystics. They killed the woman, stole her genius, and erased her name.

It took until 1946 for a female scholar, Romana Guarnieri, to find the Latin manuscripts in the Vatican and prove the book was Marguerite’s. Six hundred years the book of a burned witch was attributed to men.
Whether one sees her as a Beguine, a mystic adjacent to the movement, or both, her execution became a warning about what happened to women whose spiritual beliefs exceeded what men found manageable.

Soon after, the Council of Vienne moved against certain Beguine and Beghard beliefs and communities, especially those considered unregulated or doctrinally suspect. Not every Beguine house vanished. Some continued for centuries. But the mood had changed. Tolerance became conditional. Female independence now required explanation.

This pattern would repeat across Europe in different forms. Women who lived outside expected supervision, widows with assets, healers, solitary women, quarrelsome women, women who answered to no obvious man, could become targets of rumor, resentment, or accusation. Witch persecutions were never one simple conspiracy; they emerged from overlapping forces: misogyny, religious panic, local feuds, lots of property disputes, and state power. But again and again, the socially uncontained woman proved vulnerable.
The accusation was not always witchcraft. Sometimes it was heresy.
Sometimes immorality. Sometimes madness. Sometimes merely eccentricity.
The label changed with the century, as needed.
What threatened authority was never their belief. It was their proof of concept.
Women living together. Women supporting women. Women surviving without male management. Women demonstrating, in public, that dependence was not destiny.

The Malleus Maleficarum, the witch-hunters’ manual published in 1487, explicitly names women who “live alone or with other women” as prime suspects, because they were unaccounted for. Independence was the crime.

While the ultimate thing a woman accused of witchcraft could lose was her life, it’s not a surprise that her house, land, tools, dowry, debts, and labor often flowed back into systems already run by men: courts, landlords, churches, husbands, brothers, sons. Whether or not greed lit the first spark, patriarchy was frequently waiting with a bucket.
And make no mistake, even though patriarchy is no longer burning women at stake today, it still has weapons to try and subdue us.

Patriarchy no longer needs fire when it has a legislature. It controls our bodies through laws written by men who cannot locate a uterus on a diagram. It controls our paychecks through a gap that has barely moved in forty years and a funding desert in women’s medicine so vast that for most of recorded history, the default human body in clinical research was male, meaning drugs were tested on men, dosages calculated for men, symptoms catalogued from men, and women were left to figure out the difference on our own, in our own bodies, when it was already too late. “Lose some weight”, “it must be hormones”, these are the specialized feminine treatments we’re all so sick of.

Patriarchy controls our safety through a justice system where 98% of rapists never spend a single day in jail. Not on a technicality. Most police officers, prosecutors and judges are still male, and “boys will be boys”, or “he said, she said” will always find their way into boring cases like a rape.

And then we have the algorithm, that modern control wand that buries inconvenient ideas and surfaces convenient men. The one that hands a megaphone to Andrew Tate, the architect of modern rape culture, the man who built an empire on the premise that women are property and abuse is a business model, and calls it free speech. Substack hosts him and collects the revenue. The platform that will host this very post also hosts the man who teaches other men it’s OK to rape us.
So yeah, they didn’t stop burning women. They just made the fire digital, and handed it a Terms of Service.

Dead Women Society is not a history blog. It’s an excavation. We look at one woman, or one group of women, who built something, wrote something, invented something, lived something, and had it taken from her, hidden from the world or mocked for. Had her name filed under a man’s. Had her body or her work burned. Had her independence pathologized. Had her death not recorded.

We start with the Beguines because they are the precedent we were never taught. They prove that sisterage is not a modern feminist invention. It is a reclamation of a structure men destroyed because it worked too well.
This is what we dig. Feel free to reach out if you want to contribute your own essay or become a regular.
